article.title: How to Replace a Light Fixture Safely
article.summary: Replace a ceiling or wall light on an existing box: kill and verify the power, check the box and wiring, connect the new fixture and mount it securely.
article.body:
Swapping a dated light for a new one on the same box is a common DIY electrical job. This guide covers flush mounts, semi-flush mounts, pendants and wall sconces on existing boxes. Ceiling fans and heavy chandeliers need a box rated for them.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: switch off the breaker, not just the wall switch, and confirm the wires are dead with a non-contact tester. Use a helper or a fixture hook to hold the new light while you wire it. Stop if wire insulation is brittle, crumbly or scorched.

Steps

  1. Turn off the power and verify it

    Turn the light on, then switch off breakers until it goes out. Remove the globe and bulbs and the old fixture's mounting screws, and lower the fixture. Test every wire in the box with a non-contact voltage tester.

    Done right: the tester stays silent on every wire, after you've confirmed it works on a live outlet.

  2. Note and disconnect the wiring

    Photograph the connections. Usually black goes to black, white to white, and bare or green copper to the ground. Unscrew the wire nuts and separate the old fixture's wires.

    Done right: the house wires are separated and you have a photo of the original connections.

  3. Check the box and the wire insulation

    The box must be firmly attached to the framing. Fixtures heavier than about 50 lb and all ceiling fans need a box marked for that use. Look at the house wires: in older homes, heat from old fixtures can make insulation brittle. Many new fixtures require supply wires rated for 90°C; check the label inside the fixture.

    Done right: the box doesn't move when you push on it, and the wire insulation is flexible and intact.

  4. Install the mounting bracket

    Screw the new fixture's crossbar or bracket to the box with the screws provided. Connect the house ground wire to the green screw on the bracket, along with the fixture's ground wire.

    Done right: the bracket is tight, and the ground wires are attached to the green screw.

  5. Connect the wires

    Strip the fixture wires if needed so about 1/2 in of copper shows. Twist each pair together inside a wire nut: black (or smooth-insulation) fixture wire to the black house wire, white (or ribbed) fixture wire to the white house wire. Tug each wire to confirm it's held.

    Done right: no bare copper shows below any wire nut, and every wire stays put when tugged.

  6. Mount the fixture and test

    Fold the wires into the box, lift the fixture into place, and fasten it to the bracket. Install bulbs no higher than the fixture's maximum wattage, then the globe or shade. Turn the breaker back on and test the switch.

    Done right: the light works from the switch and the canopy sits tight to the ceiling or wall.

Call a licensed electrician if: the wires are brittle or scorched, there's no ground and the fixture needs one, the box is loose or missing, you find aluminum wiring, or you want to add a new light, switch or circuit. Rules for homeowner electrical work vary, so check with your local building department.

FAQ

Can I replace a light fixture myself?

In many areas homeowners may replace a fixture on an existing box in their own home, but rules vary. Check your local requirements.

What if there is no ground wire?

Some fixtures can still be installed safely, but the right option depends on the box and wiring. An electrician can advise.

Which wire is hot on a light fixture?

On most fixtures the smooth or black wire connects to the black house wire, and the ribbed or white wire connects to the white house wire.

Can I hang a ceiling fan where a light was?

Only if the box is rated for fan support. Most standard light boxes aren't, so you'd need a fan-rated box and brace.
